## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Tipallatthamigajātaka* (Ja 16), translated as "The Deer With Three Ruses" [SuttaCentral] or denoting the "deer in three postures" [Crosby 2014], is a birth story belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to its commentary, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at the Badarika Monastery in Kosambī concerning the Elder Rāhula's earnest desire for monastic training and obedience (*sikkhākāmo*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877; Sarao and Long 2017]. The commentary links the narrative's background to an incident at the Aggāḷava shrine near Āḷavī, where Rāhula spent the night in the Buddha's privy to scrupulously comply with monastic rules concerning shared lodgings [Fausböll 1877; Ratanamalai 2007].
Scholars observe that this tale exemplifies how Jātaka stories function as instructional models for monastic conduct, specifically guiding relations between novices and senior monastics [Crosby 2014]. In the story of the past, Rāhula is born as a young fawn entrusted by his mother to his uncle, a wise head stag (the Bodhisatta), for education [Fausböll 1877; Crosby 2014]. When ensnared in a hunter's trap, the fawn successfully feigns death and escapes by executing three strategic postures taught by his teacher [Crosby 2014]. Concluding the narrative, the Buddha connects the birth (*samodhāna*), identifying the obedient fawn as Rāhula, the mother as Uppalavaṇṇā, and the teacher stag as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877].
SuttaCentral registers no cross-language parallels for the text, and DharmaNexus similarly finds no cross-language matches with a score of 10 or greater [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus records five text-reuse matches between the canonical verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Paṭhamo bhāgo), the longest spanning verses 1.2–2.1 against commentary text (§1199–1201_0) with a 0.91 similarity score [DharmaNexus].
